Use PROCTOR from your coding agent (ADVISOR)#

This page is for developers whose coding agent runs ADVISOR, the stack's read-only MCP server. PROCTOR ships an ADVISOR module, so the agent can ask PROCTOR two questions without leaving its sandbox: "which rules do you check, and which ones block a deploy?" and "what do you say about this app right now?" Both answers come from PROCTOR's own classes. Next, see Checks for every check in prose and Deploy gate for the deploy-time rule set.

Install ADVISOR#

In the app, install ADVISOR as a dev dependency:

composer require --dev waynestate/advisor

Then add one line to the app's modules.json (or point ADVISOR_MODULES_FILE at a file that holds it):

{
    "modules": [
        "Waynestate\\Proctor\\Advisor\\ProctorModule"
    ]
}

PROCTOR does not require ADVISOR, and ADVISOR does not require PROCTOR: the module only loads when both are installed and modules.json names it.

The two read-only tools#

Both tools run in-process: no subprocess, no network, nothing written, and neither reads .env itself (four checks that do run read other env files, and only the ones git lists; see What is skipped, and why). proctor_rules takes no arguments. proctor_check takes exactly one, path: the app folder, inside the project root (default: the root itself). A path outside the root, or one that is not a folder, is refused.

proctor_rules#

proctor_rules lists every check PROCTOR registers, in the order a report prints them, straight from CheckSet. It returns proctor_version and rules, one entry per check:

  • id: the check id, for example php-floor.
  • rule_id: its rule id, proctor/<id>. A check may report named rules under it (proctor/<id>/<rule>); the Rule ids page lists them all.
  • in_gate: true when proctor gate runs the check at deploy time.
  • docs: the docs page that explains it.

One rule, as it comes back:

{
    "id": "lock-committed",
    "rule_id": "proctor/lock-committed",
    "in_gate": true,
    "docs": "https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#lock-committed"
}

proctor_check#

proctor_check runs PROCTOR's checks on the app folder with PROCTOR's own CheckRunner, the way proctor check runs them by default: the CREED policy PROCTOR bundles, today's date and the app's policy-overrides.json when it has one. It returns:

  • findings: each with rule_id, status (pass, info, warning or fail), message, file and line (null when the finding is about the app as a whole). Overrides are already applied, as in a report.
  • counts: the number of findings per status.
  • verdict: fail when any finding fails, else pass.
  • skipped: the checks it left out, each with id and reason (see below).
  • skipped_files: the env files a check that ran did not open because git does not list them, each with id (the check), file (relative to the app) and reason (see below). Empty when every env file on disk is tracked.
  • ran, app and source: what ran, on which folder (relative to the root), against which policy and for which date.

A missing or malformed composer.json or policy-overrides.json comes back as a tool error with PROCTOR's own message, the same one proctor check prints before it exits 2.

What is skipped, and why#

Some checks cannot run inside ADVISOR's sandbox, so proctor_check leaves them out and lists them under skipped:

Check Reason What it would run
composer-audit starts a subprocess composer audit
composer-version starts a subprocess composer --version
instant-client-committed starts a subprocess git, to see what is committed
lock-tracked starts a subprocess git, to see whether composer.lock is committed
wayneui-forked-views starts a subprocess git ls-files
wayneui-outdated starts a subprocess composer show (which asks Packagist) and git
node-eol, env-outside-config, raw-identity-header, robots-txt, served-folder, world-writable starts a subprocess git ls-files, to grade only committed files
override-approver starts a subprocess git blame, to see who wrote each override
app-key, vite-secrets reads .env reads committed env files for an APP_KEY, or for VITE_ variables that look like secrets

Four checks that do run read env files other than .env. Inside ADVISOR every one of them grades an env file only when git lists it, the rule app-key and vite-secrets follow in a full run, so the .env.production on a developer's laptop, which can hold real secrets, is never opened:

Check Files it reads, when git lists them What it reads in them
mysql-eol, mysql-minimum .env.squire.example, .env.example the SQUIRE_MYSQL_IMAGE= line
app-debug .env.production, .env.squire.example the APP_DEBUG value
csp-unsafe-inline .env.example, .env.production, .env.squire.example the HELMET_CSP= lines

To know what git lists without starting git, PROCTOR reads the repository's index file in PHP (the same list git ls-files prints), from the first .git folder or .git file at or above the app folder. A file on disk that the index does not list is not opened and comes back under skipped_files, with the reason not tracked by git, or no git index to read when there is no repository or its index is in a shape PROCTOR does not read (a split index). Add the file with git add, or run vendor/bin/proctor check, to have it graded.

None of them reads .env. A finding names the file and the line; the MySQL checks add the engine and version from the image name, and no other value from these files comes back. vendor/bin/proctor check reads these files from disk whether git lists them or not, as it always has: in CI the checkout holds only what the repository holds. An override in policy-overrides.json for a skipped check is not reported as unused, since its check did not run.

So a pass from proctor_check is a partial pass. Run vendor/bin/proctor check for every check, or ADVISOR's own run_proctor_check tool, which starts PROCTOR as a subprocess under ADVISOR's allowlist.

Note

The agent reports; PROCTOR decides. Every answer names its source and says plainly what ran and what did not, and the run in CI is the one that passes or fails a build. A practice paper is a fine way to study, but it is not the exam.
